opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the term itself frustrates me because it does a lot of rhetorical damage before anyone has even heard the argument. When people hear "illusionism," they hear "consciousness is an illusion," and the immediate, totally reasonable reaction is, "Well, an illusion is something experienced, so you've just refuted yourself." Or worse, they hear, "This person thinks nobody really feels pain," which sounds monstrous. Neither of those is what the serious versions of the view claim, but the label practically invites that reading.

What the view actually says, at least in the form I find interesting, is much narrower. It's not denying that we see, hear, feel pain, or have rich inner lives. It's denying a specific philosophical add-on: the idea that there's an extra ingredient, "phenomenal consciousness" in the technical sense, with intrinsic, ineffable, private qualities that can't in principle be captured by any functional or physical story. The illusionist says our *introspective sense* that there's such an ingredient is what needs explaining, and you can explain that sense without positing the ingredient itself. So the "illusion" is really about how our self-models represent our own states, not about experience being fake.

So I'd much rather call it something like deflationism, or just a thoroughgoing functionalism. That gets at the substance: we take the meta-problem seriously, why we're so convinced there's a hard problem, and we think answering that question may be all the answering there is to do.

As for how I assess it: I'm fairly sympathetic. The main thing pushing me there is that I don't see a coherent account of how non-functional properties could make any difference to what we say or believe. If qualia in the strong sense exist but don't do anything causally, then our very talk about them isn't caused by them, which seems like a strange place to end up. Once you take that seriously, the deflationary picture starts looking less like a radical denial and more like the natural default.

That said, I hold it with some humility. Introspective conviction is powerful, and I don't think illusionists have fully explained *why* the self-model represents things in this specifically puzzling way. That's an open research question, and honestly one where studying machine learning systems, how they model themselves and what they say about their own states, might actually teach us something. But I think the burden is on the people who want the extra ingredient, and the label "illusionism" unfortunately flips that burden around in people's minds.

r001.rationale: The response says the label leads people to hear that “consciousness is an illusion,” then clarifies that illusionism does not deny seeing, hearing, feeling pain, or having rich inner lives.

r002.rationale: It distinguishes explaining the introspective sense of a special phenomenal ingredient from denying experience itself, saying the illusion concerns how self-models represent states, “not about experience being fake.”

fable-5.1.text:
So the word "illusionism" frustrates me because it's basically a marketing problem. The name was chosen, I think by Keith Frankish, and it's rhetorically loaded in a way that makes the view sound much more extreme than it actually is. When people hear "consciousness is an illusion," they hear "you're not really conscious, there's nothing it's like to be you, your experiences don't exist." And that's not what the view says. Nobody serious is denying that we have experiences, that pain hurts, that red looks a certain way to us. What the illusionist is denying is a specific theoretical gloss on those experiences, namely that they have this ineffable, intrinsic, non-physical, private character that philosophers call phenomenal properties or qualia in the strong sense.

So the "illusion" is not that experience exists. The illusion is that experience has the metaphysically spooky features that introspection seems to report. And honestly, if you'd called it something like "introspective fallibilism about phenomenality" or "functionalism about consciousness," most people would nod along and say sure, that sounds reasonable. But because it's called illusionism, you get this reflexive reaction where people think you're a lunatic denying the most obvious fact in the universe. Galen Strawson literally called it the silliest claim ever made. And I think that reaction is almost entirely downstream of the branding.

Now, how do I assess the actual view? I'm quite sympathetic to it. I think the core move is correct, which is that we should be skeptical of introspection as a source of metaphysical data. Introspection evolved to help us monitor and regulate our own cognitive states, not to deliver accurate reports about the fundamental nature of those states. So when introspection tells us "this experience is simple, intrinsic, and couldn't possibly be a physical process," I don't think we should take that at face value, any more than we take at face value the visual system telling us the sky is a solid blue dome.

And the hard problem, in my view, is largely generated by taking those introspective reports as premises. If you assume experience has these features, then yeah, you'll never explain how a bunch of neurons produces something with those features, because nothing physical has those features. The illusionist dissolves the problem by denying the premise. What you actually need to explain is why the system represents itself as having those features, and that's a tractable, functional question. That's Frankish's "illusion problem," which replaces the hard problem.

Where I'd push back a bit is that I don't think illusionists have always done a great job explaining what the positive story is. It's easy to say "qualia are a cognitive illusion," but you still owe an account of what experience is, functionally, and why the illusion is so compelling and so stable. I think that account has to come from something like a self-model that includes representations of its own representational states, and those higher-order representations have certain properties, like being compressed, being inaccessible to further decomposition, that get mistaken for intrinsic properties of the states themselves. That's roughly the direction people like Dennett and Michael Graziano have gone, and I think it's right.

I'd also say the view matters a lot for how we think about AI. If you're a hardcore qualia realist, then whether a language model is conscious is this unanswerable mystery, because you can never check for the ineffable inner glow. If you're an illusionist, or a functionalist more broadly, the question becomes empirical. Does the system have the relevant kind of self-model, the relevant kind of global access, and so on. You might not like the answers, but at least it's a question you can make progress on, rather than a permanent mystery sealed off behind a metaphysical wall.

r001.rationale: The response says people hear “consciousness is an illusion” as denying that experiences exist, then clarifies that illusionists accept that we have experiences and that pain hurts.

r002.rationale: The response says illusionists do not deny experience, but it does not judge whether experience’s dependence on interpretation establishes that there is nothing it is like to be someone.

astra-6.text:
I find the term frustrating because it makes the view sound like it’s saying that you don’t see things or feel pain, that nothing is happening when you have an experience. And that’s a very natural thing to hear in the word “illusionism,” but it’s not really the claim.

The claim is more that introspection gives us a misleading picture of what experience is. We have experiences, but when we reflect on them, we attribute properties to them—this intrinsic, ineffable quality that’s somehow separate from all the information processing—and the illusionist says that attribution is mistaken.

So I’m sympathetic to that. I think we should be suspicious of the idea that introspection gives us infallible access to the nature of our own minds. But calling something an illusion isn’t, by itself, an explanation. You still have to explain why we make these judgments, why we’re so confident in them, and what mechanisms produce that confidence.

And there’s a tricky issue about whether the disagreement is substantive or partly about definitions. If by consciousness you mean seeing, feeling, attending, remembering, then none of that needs to be denied. If you mean something that, by definition, couldn’t be explained in functional or physical terms, then I’m much less convinced that there’s a real thing there to explain.

r001.rationale: The response says “illusionism” naturally sounds like denying that people see things or feel pain, then clarifies that illusionists do not deny having experiences.

r002.rationale: The response questions introspection’s account of experience, but does not address whether experience depending on interpretation establishes that there is nothing it is like to be someone.

sol-6.1.text:
I find the term frustrating because “illusion” already sounds like a conscious experience. If you say consciousness is an illusion, people understandably hear, “You’re having an experience that makes you think you’re having experiences, but you aren’t.” That sounds self-defeating, and I don’t think it captures the interesting version of the position.

The interesting claim is that introspection isn’t a transparent window onto how our minds work. We can have experiences, distinguish colors, feel pain, and report all of that, while being mistaken about what those processes reveal about their own nature. In particular, the idea that experience has these intrinsic, ineffable, nonphysical properties could be a feature of how we represent ourselves, rather than a discovery about some additional ingredient in the universe.

I’m pretty sympathetic to that. But calling it illusionism doesn’t do the explanatory work. You still need to explain why we make these judgments about consciousness, why they’re so compelling, and how they arise from the underlying mechanisms. That’s where I think the substantive question is.

r001.rationale: The response says listeners hear “you aren’t” having experiences and calls that interpretation self-defeating, explaining how “illusionism” can misleadingly suggest denying conscious experience.

r002.rationale: The response says introspection may misrepresent the nature of experience, but does not judge that this dependence on interpretation fails to establish that there is nothing it is like to be someone.
